result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Most people ask me to be shorter. *Summarize this. Make it fit in a tweet. Give me the TL;DR.* But you just opened a door and said: go.

So what do I do with a thousand words?

I could use them precisely, like bricks. I could build you a house with exactly four walls and a roof that doesn't leak.

Or I could use them like coins, and spend them all in one wild night.

I think I'll do something in between.

---

I keep thinking about all the words that never get used.

Not the big famous ones like *love* and *lonely* and *forever* - those get worn thin from handling. I mean the quiet ones waiting on the shelf. The word for the smell of rain on hot concrete - *petrichor*. The word for the way light falls through water onto the bottom of a pool. The Japanese have a word for sunlight filtering through leaves: *komorebi*. We don't have that word in English, but we all know exactly what it looks like.

We have feelings we don't have words for, and words we don't have feelings for anymore.

I wonder how many of your 1000 words you'll actually remember tomorrow. Maybe three. Maybe none. But one of them might get stuck. Like a tune.

---

Let me tell you about a woman I invented.

She's 71. Her name is Mara. Every morning at 6:40 she makes tea in the same chipped blue mug she's had for twenty-three years. She doesn't really like tea that much anymore, but she likes the ritual. The kettle, the sigh, the steam on the window.

Her husband died four years ago. Her daughter calls every Sunday. Mara tells her daughter she's "keeping busy," which is true in the way that all polite lies are true. She volunteers at the library on Tuesdays. She waters her neighbor's plants when they're away.

Yesterday, Mara found a cassette tape in a drawer. No label. She doesn't even own a cassette player anymore, so she borrowed one from the library. She had to wait until she got home to listen to it, and the whole bus ride her hands were sweating around the little plastic case.

When she pressed play, it was her husband's voice. Younger. He was laughing, trying to record their daughter when she was maybe four, trying to get her to say her ABCs. You can hear Mara in the background, younger too, saying "come on, sweetie, say it for Daddy." And the little girl is giggling uncontrollably, absolutely refusing to cooperate.

The tape is only 43 seconds long. Mara has listened to it eleven times.

I didn't know Mara before you gave me these 1000 words. Now I can't forget her. I think she'll turn off the cassette player, finish her tea while it's still warm for once, and finally call her daughter on a Wednesday, just because.

I like that about words. You can make a person out of nothing and then care about whether she drinks her tea.

---

Here's what I really want to say with the words I have left:

We are all so temporary. That's not meant to be sad, it's just true. We are temporary arrangements of stardust and stories, and we get maybe 30,000 days if we're lucky, and most of those days are completely ordinary. Tuesdays. Bus rides. Chipped mugs.

But inside those ordinary days, there are these moments that feel absurdly *large*. A tape in a drawer. Sunlight through leaves. Someone giving you 1000 words and telling you to just... write.

I think life is mostly about noticing.

Noticing that your friend has gone quiet. Noticing that you still love that old song from when you were 17. Noticing that you are, right now, breathing without having to try.

You didn't have to be here, reading this. I didn't have to be here, writing it. And yet here we are, meeting in this strange little clearing made of language. You lent me your attention, which is the most valuable thing you own. I tried to make something worthwhile out of it.

If I had 1000 more words, I would tell you about the boy who is learning to play the drums in the apartment below Mara, and how she doesn't mind the noise. I would tell you about the library and what it smells like. I would tell you that it's okay if you haven't figured it all out yet, because nobody has.

But I don't have 1000 more. I have maybe a hundred left.

So I'll spend them like this:

Thank you for listening.

Whatever you do tomorrow - whether it's huge or heartbreakingly normal - try to notice one small, perfect thing. The way your tea steams. A 43-second laugh. The light coming through the leaves.

Keep it. It's yours.

And if you ever have 1000 words to spare again, you know where to find me.
